summary: The strawberry tree is an evergreen shrub or small tree native to the Mediterranean Basin and western Europe, although its native status in Ireland is uncertain. Its rough, red berries take about a year to mature, so autumn fruit can appear alongside the next season’s white, bell-shaped flowers. Birds disperse its seeds, and people use the fruit fresh, in preserves and in alcoholic drinks such as Portuguese medronho.
reviewFlags: Irish native status remains uncertain in s1:p16.
The bear-intoxication claim in s1:p52 is marked citation needed (June 2011); it does not establish toxicity to people.
The suggestion in s1:p37 that bees might modify unedone to reduce possible toxic effects is speculative, not an established poisoning report.

summary: Cork oak is an evergreen tree native to southwestern Europe and northwestern Africa. Its thick, spongy bark supplies cork for bottle stoppers, flooring and insulation. The cork layer regenerates, allowing repeated harvests, typically beginning at about twenty-five years and recurring every nine to twelve years. The same bark can insulate the tree during forest fires, helping it survive and rebuild its crown.
reviewFlags: The fire-recovery claim in s1:p21 carries a citation-needed warning (October 2023), although s1:p24 also describes the mechanism.

summary: Sea fig is a creeping, mat-forming succulent native to South Africa. Its yellow flowers open in bright morning sunlight and close at night, while fruit-eating mammals disperse its seeds. Early twentieth-century California plantings used it to stabilise dunes and soil beside railways. It has since become invasive there, as well as in Australia and the Mediterranean, where dense stands compete with other plants for water, nutrients, light and space.
reviewFlags: The South African fresh-fruit and jam claim in s1:p23 is marked citation needed (November 2020).
The invasiveness description in s1:p12 has regional scope but no assessment date.

summary: Bermuda buttercup is a yellow-flowered, bulb-producing wood sorrel native to South Africa. Native populations have three flower forms with different stigma heights, but many introduced populations produce no seed and spread vegetatively through abundant small bulbs. It is described as invasive in places including coastal California and Australia. It also has traditional food uses in South Africa, while fatal poisoning has been reported when hungry livestock gorge on it in South Australia.
reviewFlags: The source has a references-improvement warning dated June 2026.

The hazards section beginning at s1:p15 is marked original research (November 2012). The large-quantity toxicity claim carries a citation-needed warning (September 2010), and the kidney-stone discussion carries citation-needed warnings (November 2020).
Food-use and risk-reduction claims in s1:p15 need further review; the passage does not verify a safe preparation or quantity.
The modest-quantity harmlessness claim in s1:p19 is conditional and does not negate the large-intake livestock poisoning reports.

summary: The bee orchid is a perennial herb whose hairy lower petal resembles a bee. In the Mediterranean, male solitary bees can transfer pollen while attempting to mate with flowers that mimic female bees in both appearance and scent. Farther north, the flowers almost exclusively pollinate themselves. It grows on nutrient-poor calcareous soils in grassland, open woodland and disturbed sites such as old quarries, relying on symbiotic fungi for nutrients.
reviewFlags: s1:p17 attributes historical salep production to this species but discusses modern salep generically; the species attribution of the food-use claim needs further review.
The historical nutritional, medicinal and aphrodisiac values in s1:p17 are reported beliefs, not evidence of therapeutic efficacy.

summary: Armeria gaditana is a flowering plant in the Plumbaginaceae family, endemic to the southwestern Iberian Peninsula. In Portugal it inhabits meadows with somewhat damp, sandy soils in the eastern Algarve. Its mainland Portuguese population was classified as Critically Endangered in a 2020 assessment based on work from 2016–2019; just one adult plant was then known nationally. Changes to soil water conditions were a pressure at its remaining locality.
reviewFlags: The conservation category, single-adult count and habitat pressures describe the 2020 regional publication, based on assessments in 2016–2019; their current status is not established by these passages.

summary: Cook pine is a conifer endemic to New Caledonia, with a narrow, spire-like crown and short branches arranged in whorls. Its needle-like young leaves give way to broader, scale-like adult foliage. Its lean also varies with location: in a 2017 study, trees tended to lean southward in the Northern Hemisphere and northward in the Southern Hemisphere, while those on the Equator grew upright.
